items.a:
2PC (prepare → commit via coordinator) suffers from:
- [[r:blocking]]: participants hold resource locks from prepare through commit; if the coordinator dies, they're stuck in-doubt indefinitely
- [[r:poor availability]]: one slow participant stalls the whole transaction
- [[r:doesn't scale]]: holding locks across the network, tight coupling

:::tip Bottom line
modern distributed systems trade 'distributed atomicity' for [[g:controlled eventual consistency]] via Saga + Outbox + idempotency.
:::

:::deep
- the prepare phase holds *resource locks* until commit (blocking other transactions); if the coordinator dies after prepare, the participant is stuck [[r:in-doubt]] (holding the lock indefinitely, unable to decide on its own) — needs manual intervention
- one slow/failing participant stalls the whole transaction (poor availability, doesn't scale)

2PC is only appropriate in a narrow, homogeneous scope (XA between DB+JMS within a single service), [[r:not for long-running business flows spanning multiple services]] like OTA booking.
:::

items.q: Saga: choreography vs orchestration? Compensating transaction?
items.a: [[g:Saga]]: split a long transaction into a chain of local transactions; if a step fails, run a [[g:compensating transaction]] (a business-level undo, e.g. a reversing entry — not an actual DB rollback). - [[b:Choreography]]: services publish/listen to events, no conductor — loose coupling, but the overall flow is hard to see at a glance - [[b:Orchestration]]: an orchestrator drives each step — clear flow, easier to monitor/handle errors, at the cost of a central point Compensation must be [[o:idempotent]] and safe to run multiple times. :::warn Note Saga = eventual consistency → there's a window of 'imbalance'. The UI/business logic must accept a PENDING state, [[r:never act on a balance that hasn't settled]]. ::: :::deep - needs a [[g:saga log/state store]] (the orchestrator tracks which step it's on) to recover after a crash and resume; every step + its compensation must be idempotent - compensation isn't always feasible (an email already sent, a real ticket already issued) → use a [[o:pivot transaction]]: order the 'irreversible' steps last, so after the pivot point only forward progress is possible, no going back OTA: hold a seat (reversible) → charge payment (reversible via refund) → issue the ticket through the GDS (hard to reverse → placed last). The intermediate state exposed to the UI is PENDING/PROCESSING. :::

items.q: The Outbox pattern, and why is dual-write dangerous?
items.a: [[r:Dual write]] (writing to the DB and publishing to the broker as separate steps) → if either side fails they drift out of sync: the DB says the money was transferred but the other service never received the event. [[g:Outbox]]: write the event to an outbox table *in the same transaction* as the business change → atomic; a publisher (CDC/polling) reads the outbox and publishes (at-least-once → consumer must be idempotent). :::tip Tie to your background Publisher Confirms (broker acknowledges receipt) + Outbox (atomic DB↔publish) together close the gap. ::: :::deep - dual-write is dangerous because the DB and the broker/HTTP call don't share a transaction → they fall out of sync when one side fails, and the bug is hard to catch (only surfaces on rare network failures) - Outbox turns it into *one* atomic local DB write (state + event in the same tx), pushing the 'publish externally' part to an async publisher (retries until delivery succeeds, then marks it SENT) OTA: [[r:avoid `save(booking); kafka.send(event)`]] — if the send fails after commit, ticketing never learns the booking is PAID. Outbox + CDC (Debezium) is the standard way to 'reliably publish events' without blocking the business flow waiting on the broker. - Decide *what* is allowed into the outbox: an integration event with a public, versioned contract — not an internal domain event (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3). :::

items.q: How does TCC (Try-Confirm-Cancel) differ from Saga?
items.a:
TCC splits each operation into 3 phases: - [[b:Try]]: reserve/hold a resource in advance (e.g. freeze an amount of money) - [[b:Confirm]]: actually apply the change on top of what was held - [[b:Cancel]]: release the held resource if something fails
SagaTCC
Approachdo it for real, then compensatereserve first, confirm later
Intermediate statevisible externallyhidden (just 'held')
Isolationweakerbetter
Cost1 op + 1 compensation3 idempotent phases per service
:::deep - Saga *compensates after the fact* (money is deducted first, then refunded if needed); TCC *reserves up front* → avoids exposing intermediate state, better isolation - trade-off: every service must implement all 3 idempotent phases plus manage the 'reservation' (auto-release via TTL if it hangs) OTA: seat-hold is exactly TCC (Try=hold the seat with a TTL, Confirm=issue the ticket, Cancel=release); payment = Try=authorize (hold the funds), Confirm=capture, Cancel=void — this matches the PSP authorize/capture model exactly. :::

items.q: Two services need to stay consistent without a distributed transaction — what are the options?
items.a:
In order of preference:
- [[g:Merge into one bounded context]]: if the two pieces of data need strong consistency (both legs of a ledger entry) → put them in the same service/DB, local ACID. [[r:Don't split into microservices just because it's fashionable.]]
- [[b:Saga + Outbox]] if a split is unavoidable: accept eventual consistency + compensation
- [[b:Idempotency + retry]] on every step
- [[b:Reconciliation]] jobs to periodically detect & fix drift

:::tip Key takeaway
'service boundaries should follow consistency boundaries'. If two things must be atomic with each other, that's a signal they belong in the same service.
:::

:::deep
- (1) merge the bounded context if strong consistency is required (both legs of a ledger entry, holding a seat + decrementing inventory) → local ACID
- (2) if a split is unavoidable → Saga + Outbox + eventual consistency + compensation
- (3) idempotency + retry on every step; (4) periodic reconciliation to fix drift

OTA: 'hold seat' + 'decrement inventory' should live in the same Inventory service (atomic); 'booking' + 'payment' can be split (Saga).

[[r:A misplaced boundary is the root cause of a distributed monolith.]]
:::

items.q: Distributed lock (Redis/Redlock) — when to use it, and what are the risks?
items.a:
Used to serialize an operation across instances (only one worker runs the job): `SET key val NX PX ttl`.

[[r:Risk]]: the TTL expires before processing finishes → two holders enter at once.

Mitigations:
- [[g:fencing token]] (a monotonically increasing number; the resource rejects an older token)
- keep the critical section short

:::warn Fintech
don't rely SOLELY on a distributed lock for money correctness. Let the DB be the final arbiter (unique constraint, optimistic locking, conditional update); [[o:the lock only reduces contention]].
:::

:::deep
- `SET key val NX PX ttl` for mutual exclusion across instances
- [[r:fatal risk]]: the TTL expires before processing finishes → two holders enter the critical section at once → [[g:fencing token]] (the resource rejects a token older than one it has already seen)
- Redlock (multi-node) is controversial (Kleppmann) — clock skew/GC pauses can still break its safety guarantees

Fintech: [[r:do NOT rely solely on a lock for money/seat correctness]] — let the DB be the final arbiter (unique constraint, optimistic version, conditional update); the lock only *reduces contention*. Lock for 'coordination', DB for 'correctness'.
:::

items.q: Real-world scenario: a call to a PSP/bank times out and you don't know whether the money was already deducted?
items.a:
[[r:Unknown state]] — never default to assuming failure or success.

- send every PSP call with an [[g:idempotency key]] from the start → safe retries, no double-charging
- on timeout → mark it `UNKNOWN/PENDING`, [[r:do NOT tell the user it succeeded]]
- [[g:status query/inquiry]] to the PSP, or wait for the webhook, to learn the real outcome
- end-of-day [[g:reconciliation]] against the settlement file to close out pending transactions; have a business-level timeout + auto-reversal

:::tip Bottom line
'when unsure, don't guess — query again and reconcile'. Idempotency + reconciliation are the safety net of every payment system.
:::

:::deep
- calls to the GDS (Amadeus/Sabre) or a PSP can both time out in an indeterminate state
- invariant rule: every outbound call carries an idempotency key (or reuses booking_id/order_id), stored as `PENDING`, [[r:never infer success on your own]]
- after a timeout: call a *retrieve/status API* (GDS PNR lookup; PSP inquiry) or wait for the webhook; run reconciliation against the end-of-day settlement file; have a *business-level timeout* + auto-void/refund once it expires

This is exactly the kind of 'real-world challenge' that fits well into a 'most challenging project' story.
:::

items.q: Idempotency in payments: how do you implement it airtight?
items.a:
The client sends an [[g:Idempotency-Key]] with every payment intent. The server stores key→result; a duplicate request returns the stored result instead of executing again. 
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys(key,status,response)
VALUES(?, 'IN_PROGRESS', NULL);  -- unique violation => retry
Store the key + result in the *same tx* as the business change (or via outbox) → no gap where 'the action ran but the key wasn't saved'. Handle the IN_PROGRESS state when a duplicate request arrives early. :::deep - server, within *one transaction*: INSERT the key (unique, IN_PROGRESS) → a unique violation means a duplicate request → return the stored result (or 409 if still IN_PROGRESS) - perform the business logic + store the response tied to the key in the same tx (or via outbox) → [[g:no gap where 'done but key not saved']] - keys have a sensible TTL (scoped per endpoint + user) OTA: every call out to a PSP/GDS carries an idempotency key (or order_id) → safe retries, no double-charge/double-issue. Race where two duplicate requests arrive nearly simultaneously: the second one sees IN_PROGRESS → poll/wait or return 409, [[r:never execute in parallel]]. :::

items.q: Double-entry bookkeeping — why is it the gold standard for a ledger?
items.a:
Every transaction has ≥2 entries: debit + credit, [[g:sum = 0]]. Money is never created or destroyed.

The ledger is [[g:append-only/immutable]]:
- never UPDATE/DELETE a past entry
- fix mistakes with a *reversing entry* → the audit trail is baked into the design

Balance = sum of entries (or a materialized value reconciled periodically). Enforce the invariant `SUM(amount)=0` per transaction.

:::tip Bottom line
'the ledger is an immutable book of record — every change is a new entry' — a strong closing line for a fintech system.
:::

:::deep
- table `ledger_entry(id, txn_id, account_id, direction, amount, currency, created_at)`, append-only; the constraint `SUM(signed_amount) per txn_id = 0` is checked both in the app and by a reconciliation job
- balance: compute on-the-fly (`SUM` per account) or keep a materialized `account_balance` updated in the same tx + reconciled periodically
- [[r:never UPDATE/DELETE an entry]] — fix it with a *reversing entry*; add a unique `idempotency_key` to prevent duplicate writes
- multi-currency: each entry carries its currency + the exchange rate at that point in time; [[r:never mix currencies in a single sum]]
:::

items.q: Why not use float for money? What's the correct way to store it?
items.a:
Binary float/double cannot represent 0.1/0.2 exactly → [[r:accumulated rounding drift]] as values add up. Use instead: - `DECIMAL(p,s)` or minor units (cents) as a BIGINT - Java `BigDecimal` constructed from a [[o:String]] (never from a double!) - an explicit rounding mode (HALF_EVEN) - store the currency code alongside the amount, [[r:never add amounts of different currencies]] 
new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2"))
    .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); // 0.30
:::deep - binary double/float cannot represent 0.1/0.2 exactly (IEEE 754) → drift accumulates across many transactions → mismatches at reconciliation time → violates the ledger invariant - `BigDecimal` constructed from a *String* (never a double!), an explicit rounding mode (`HALF_EVEN`, 'banker's rounding', reduces bias), scale set per currency - [[r:`new BigDecimal(0.1)` (from a double) still carries the error]] — it must be `new BigDecimal("0.1")` OTA multi-currency: every `ledger_entry` carries a currency + a minor-unit amount; totals are checked per currency; rounding on currency conversion must be consistent & auditable. :::

items.q: How do you prevent double-spend / balance races under high load?
items.a:
[[r:Never 'read the balance then subtract in the app']] (a race). Let the DB make it atomic:

- [[g:conditional update]]: `UPDATE acc SET balance=balance-? WHERE id=? AND balance>=?` — 0 rows affected = insufficient funds
- [[b:optimistic locking]] (a version column) + retry; or [[b:pessimistic]] `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` under high contention
- append-only ledger: balance is derived from entries, consistency is enforced at the DB layer

:::tip Bottom line
money correctness must be anchored to DB-level constraints (atomic, unique, conditional), not app logic or a distributed lock.
:::

:::deep
Classify the business case:
- 'countable, must not go negative' (balance, seats, ticket inventory) → conditional update / optimistic
- 'must be unique' (1 seat, 1 person) → unique constraint on (flight, seat, status)

OTA seat: `UPDATE seat SET status='HELD', hold_by=?, hold_exp=now()+'7m' WHERE id=? AND status='FREE'` — atomic, 0 rows = lost the race. [[r:Avoid 'SELECT to check, then INSERT']] (a TOCTOU race).

Extremely high load on a hot flight → serialize per-flight via a queue, or bucket seats to reduce contention. An idempotency key on the booking request prevents a double 'book' click.
:::

items.q: Eventual consistency in fintech: where is it acceptable, and where is it forbidden?
items.a:
- [[r:FORBIDDEN for eventual]]: available balance used to decide spending, both legs of one ledger entry, limit checks, anti-double-spend
- [[g:ACCEPTABLE for eventual]]: displayed transaction history, notifications, reports/analytics, reward points

Principle: anywhere data is used to *make a decision about money* → must be [[g:strong consistency]].

:::deep
- FORBIDDEN for eventual: available balance used to decide spending, both legs of one ledger entry, limit checks/seat inventory checks before finalizing, anti-double-spend
- ACCEPTABLE for eventual: displayed history, notifications, analytics, reward points, displayed search/availability

OTA: showing '3 seats left' can be slightly stale (eventual, cached), but the *seat-hold/payment* step must [[g:re-validate atomically against inventory]] (strong) — [[r:never let a user pay based on stale 'seats left' data]]. Design the UI around this boundary (PENDING, re-validate at checkout).
:::
